conditions: Free unconstrained expansion in the specified direction, with small fractional length change and approximately constant linear thermal expansion coefficient. The equality denotes the first-order linear approximation, not an exact finite-temperature law.
spoken_aliases: delta l equals alpha times l sub zero times delta t
change in length equals the linear thermal expansion coefficient times initial length times the change in temperature

evidence: The linear expansion coefficient is the fractional length derivative with temperature under the specified mechanical conditions. Linearizing the length about its initial temperature gives delta L approximately alpha L0 delta T; higher-order terms are neglected.
Reference checked 2026-11-27: https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-2/pages/1-key-equations. Proposed maintainer approval, not independent human certification.
